en: Should old acquaintance be forgotten,
And never brought to mind?
Should old acquaintance be forgotten,
And the days of long ago?
For old times long ago, my dear,
For old times long ago,
We'll take a cup of kindness yet,
For old times long ago.
We two have run about the hillsides,
And pulled the pretty daisies;
But we've wandered many a weary foot,
Since old times long ago.
We two have paddled in the stream,
From morning sun till dinner-time;
But broad seas have roared between us,
Since old times long ago.
And here's a hand, my trusty friend,
And give me a hand of yours;
And we'll take a right good drink of goodwill,
For old times long ago.
And surely you'll pay for your pint-cup,
And surely I'll pay for mine;
And we'll take a cup of kindness yet,
For old times long ago.
notes: 'auld lang syne' is literally 'old long since': the old days, times long past. It is rendered 'old times long ago' throughout, and 'days o' lang syne' (1.4) as 'the days of long ago'.
line 3.1: 'braes' are hillsides or slopes, often by a river.
line 3.2: 'gowans' are daisies (or other wild field flowers); 'fine' is pretty, fine.
line 3.3: 'mony a weary foot' is literally 'many a weary foot': many a tiring step or mile; kept as written.
line 4.2: 'dine' is dinner, the midday meal in Burns's Scotland: from morning till midday.
line 5.2: 'gie's' is 'give us', in Scots usage 'give me'.
line 5.3: 'willie-waught' is a hearty drink taken together; the word comes from a misdivision of 'gude-willie waught' (a good-will draught), so its exact sense is debated.
line 6.1-2: 'ye'll be your pint-stoup' means 'you will stand for (pay for) your own tankard'; a 'stoup' is a drinking vessel. The sense 'pay for' is the usual reading, not a word-for-word one.
